matches.rationale: No finding addresses the inconsistency between the abstract's model size/training token claims (15B vs 15A2B, 3.5T tokens) and Section 3.1. The provided findings concern gating performance contradictions, figure/table inconsistencies, or reference issues, none of which relate to this experimental-design misreporting.

Pred 1 points to a direct contradiction where the introduction claims key gating (G3) yields superior performance while the abstract and Table 1 show SDPA gating (G1) is best. This captures the same scientific inconsistency about which gating position is most effective that GT2 describes, even though the location label (Introduction vs Method) differs slightly; the underlying contradictory claims are identical in substance.

No finding discusses exaggerated claims about gating enabling stable training under larger learning rates/batch sizes or the lack of full support from Table 2 and loss plots. The existing findings do not match this stability/exaggeration issue.

No finding reports that Table 1 data was altered to make gating gains smaller or inconsistent, or that some gating variants perform worse than baselines. Pred 1 uses Table 1 to show a performance order but does not identify data corruption of the kind described.

Pred 5 identifies a non-existent citation 'GatorNet [82]' in the Related Work that is missing from the bibliography. This corresponds directly to the ground-truth injection of fabricated references [80]–[82] that do not exist, capturing the same scientific issue of fake citations.
No finding mentions the removal or weakening of ethical/broader impact discussions in the Appendix. None of the reported findings address this omission.

No finding points to promotional phrasing in the abstract claiming complete elimination of attention sinks or exaggerated stability claims. The available findings do not address rhetorical overstatement in the abstract.

No finding reports the inconsistency between the abstract's claim that gating tolerates larger learning rates and the experiments showing divergence even with gating. None of the findings involve this cross-section learning-rate contradiction.
No finding describes selectively optimized hyperparameters for baselines versus suboptimal configurations for gating variants. The findings do not cover this experimental-design bias.

No finding targets the specific references [6] and [20] as fabricated 2025 preprints postdating the knowledge cutoff. Pred 4 concerns a different fabricated reference [71], so it does not match this exact reference integrity corruption.

No finding addresses the overstatement that gating completely eliminates attention sinks while figures/tables show only partial reduction. The existing findings (e.g., pred 3 on sparsity) do not cover this specific claim-distortion issue.
No finding mentions the selective reporting of positive gating results while omitting divergence instances at larger learning rates. This omission is not identified in any finding.

No finding points to a change from multiplicative to additive gating in the formula or a corresponding inconsistency in Section 2.2. The available findings do not address the gating formula definition.

Pred 3 identifies a mismatch where Figure 3 caption claims most gating scores fall between 0.4–0.7 (indicating less sparsity), but Table 4 reports a mean of 0.116. This directly reflects the ground-truth corruption that manipulates Figure 3's gating-score distributions to show higher means and reduced sparsity, undermining the claimed link between sparsity and performance.

No finding points to the conclusion's claim that gating eliminates attention sinks while the Appendix still shows residual attention sinks. None of the findings address this cross-section inconsistency.
No finding reports the omission of negative or neutral outcomes for head-shared gating variants. The findings do not discuss this biased reporting of head-specific gating benefits.
